senses.gloss:
dyūta
(‘gambling’)
------------------------------------------
Gambling with dice play seems to be an ancient pastime, especially for kings. The Ṛgveda (10.34) contains the piteous laments of a gambler. The notorious game of dice between युधिष्ठिर and शकुनि (on behalf of दुर्योधन) described in the Mahābhārata is now history, as the root-cause of the कुरुक्षेत्र war. In the पुराणस् and the धर्मशास्त्रस् there are statements of condemnation of the गम्ब्लिन्ग् with dice-play. At the same time rules to regulate it too have been described! It was perhaps necessary to control it since it existed as an unavoidable evil.
The dice pieces are made of vibhītaka wood (a kind of myrobalan).
The game has to be conducted in a public place supervised by a sabhika (who gives the place and collects some rent for it) and some expert gamblers, who will act as umpires. The defeated person has to pay a part of his loss to the king as tax which may be 5 to 10 per cent. It is the duty of the sabhika or the agents of the king to see that the stake money is paid by the losing party to the victor. In circumstances where the loser loses everything, becoming a beggar, the king prevents it by providing for the bare maintenance of the loser.
The kings used to permit गम्ब्लिन्ग् centres as one of the methods for finding out thieves and criminals.
An arranged dice-play is a ritual part of the राजसूय sacrifice.

Dyumatsena
------------------------------------------
Princess सावित्री has been highly eulogised in the Hindu mythological lore as an ideal wife, nay, the very personification of wifely virtues like chastity and singular devotion to the husband. सत्यवान् was her fortunate husband.
Dyumatsena, the king of the Sāḷva country was his ड़थेर्. Though he was devoted to धर्म and ruled well, he lost his eyesight and was conquered by a rival king who drove him out of his kingdom. He lived in a forest along with his wife and son सत्यवान्. Princess सावित्री chose to marry सत्यवान् even though she was apprised that he would die very soon.
Dyumatsena regained his eyesight and the kingdom due to सावित्री’s prayer to यम, the god of death.
See also SĀVITRĪ.
